Answer ALL the SIX questions in this booklet. The mark allocation is indicated for each question. Each question carries 20 marks. questions.enonce_markdown: Define the term "mole of a substance". *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **mole** of a substance is the amount of that substance which contains as many elementary entities (atoms, molecules, ions, electrons...) as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12. This number of entities is the Avogadro constant, $L = 6.02\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}$.

Equivalently, one mole of a substance has a mass in grams equal to its relative atomic (or molecular, or formula) mass: for example 1 mol of $\mathrm{H_2O}$ is 18.0 g and contains $6.02\times10^{23}$ molecules.

questions.enonce_markdown:
1.50 g of ethyl ethanoate was hydrolysed with 50.0 cm$^3$ of 0.5 M NaOH solution and the mixture was made up to 250 cm$^3$ with distilled water in a volumetric flask.

Calculate:

**A:** The number of moles of ethyl ethanoate in 1.50 g. (RMM: $\mathrm{CH_3CO_2C_2H_5} = 88$)

**B:** The number of moles of NaOH in 50 cm$^3$ of 0.5 M solution.

**C:** The percentage yield when 1.50 g of ethyl ethanoate reacts completely with sodium hydroxide to give 0.63 g of ethanol. (RAM: C = 12.0, H = 1.0, O = 16.0, Na = 23.0) *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**A.** $n(\text{ester}) = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{M_r} = \dfrac{1.50}{88} = 1.70\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mol}$ (0.01705 mol).

**B.** $n(\mathrm{NaOH}) = c \times V = 0.5\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}} \times \dfrac{50.0}{1000}\ \mathrm{dm^3} = 2.50\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mol}$.

(Making the mixture up to 250 cm$^3$ only dilutes it; it does not change the amounts of substance.)

**C.** Hydrolysis of the ester by alkali:

$$\mathrm{CH_3COOC_2H_5} + \mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_3COONa} + \mathrm{C_2H_5OH}$$

The mole ratio ester : NaOH : ethanol is 1 : 1 : 1. There is 0.0250 mol of NaOH for 0.0170 mol of ester, so NaOH is in excess and the **ester is the limiting reagent**: "reacts completely" means all 0.01705 mol of ester is converted.

Theoretical amount of ethanol $= 0.01705\ \mathrm{mol}$.

$M(\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}) = 2(12.0) + 6(1.0) + 16.0 = 46.0\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$

Theoretical mass of ethanol $= 0.01705 \times 46.0 = 0.784\ \mathrm{g}$.

$$\text{Percentage yield} = \frac{\text{actual mass}}{\text{theoretical mass}} \times 100 = \frac{0.63}{0.784} \times 100 = 80.3\,\%$$

The percentage yield of ethanol is about **80 %**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The following is a path of the Uranium decay series:

$${}^{238}_{92}\mathrm{U} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{A}\ } {}^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{B}\ } {}^{234}_{91}\mathrm{Pa} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{C}\ } \mathrm{X}$$

(i) Identify the particles emitted in steps A and B.

A: ........ B: ........

(ii) If a beta particle is emitted in stage C, give the atomic number and mass number of the isotope X.

Atomic number: ........ Mass number: ........

(iii) If the activity of ${}^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th}$ is reduced to 25% in 48 days. What is the half-life of ${}^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th}$? *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** In each step the mass number and the atomic number (nuclear charge) must balance.

- **Step A:** ${}^{238}_{92}\mathrm{U} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$. The mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number by 2, so A is an **alpha particle** ($\alpha$, a helium nucleus ${}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$).
- **Step B:** ${}^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{91}\mathrm{Pa} + {}^{\ 0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$. The mass number is unchanged and the atomic number rises by 1 (a neutron changes into a proton), so B is a **beta particle** ($\beta^-$, an electron ${}^{\ 0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$).

**(ii)** Beta emission from ${}^{234}_{91}\mathrm{Pa}$: ${}^{234}_{91}\mathrm{Pa} \rightarrow {}^{\ A}_{\ Z}\mathrm{X} + {}^{\ 0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$.

Mass number: $234 = A + 0$, so $A = 234$. Atomic number: $91 = Z + (-1)$, so $Z = 92$.

**Atomic number = 92, mass number = 234**: X is ${}^{234}_{92}\mathrm{U}$ (uranium-234).

**(iii)** The activity falls from 100 % to 25 %:

$$100\,\% \xrightarrow{\ t_{1/2}\ } 50\,\% \xrightarrow{\ t_{1/2}\ } 25\,\%$$

so two half-lives have elapsed: $2\,t_{1/2} = 48$ days, hence

$$t_{1/2} = \frac{48}{2} = \mathbf{24\ days}.$$

Check with the decay law: $A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$ gives $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 4}{48} = 0.0289\ \mathrm{day^{-1}}$ and $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = 24.0$ days.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The mass spectrum of a vaporized sample of chromium shows the following data:

| Mass of isotope | 50 | 52 | 53 | 54 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Relative abundance | 0.04 | 0.84 | 0.1 | 0.02 |

Calculate the relative atomic mass of chromium. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The relative atomic mass is the weighted mean of the isotopic masses:

$$A_r = \frac{\sum (\text{isotopic mass} \times \text{relative abundance})}{\sum \text{relative abundance}}$$

The abundances add up to $0.04 + 0.84 + 0.10 + 0.02 = 1.00$, so the denominator is 1.

$$A_r = (50 \times 0.04) + (52 \times 0.84) + (53 \times 0.10) + (54 \times 0.02) = 2.00 + 43.68 + 5.30 + 1.08 = 52.06$$

The relative atomic mass of chromium is **52.1** (52.06).

questions.enonce_markdown:
The following data were obtained from the reaction below:

$$2\mathrm{NO(g)} + 2\mathrm{H_2(g)} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} + \mathrm{N_2(g)}$$

| Experiment | Initial concentration: [NO] / mol dm$^{-3}$ | Initial concentration: [H$_2$] / mol dm$^{-3}$ | Relative rate of reaction |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.1 | 0.1 | 1 |
| 2 | 0.3 | 0.1 | 9 |
| 3 | 0.3 | 0.2 | 18 |

(i) Determine the order with respect to NO

(ii) Determine the order with respect to H$_2$

(iii) Write the rate expression for the reaction

(iv) Calculate the value of the rate constant. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Order with respect to NO.** Compare experiments 1 and 2: $[\mathrm{H_2}]$ is constant (0.1) and $[\mathrm{NO}]$ is multiplied by 3 ($0.1 \rightarrow 0.3$). The rate is multiplied by 9, and $3^2 = 9$. So the reaction is **second order with respect to NO**.

**(ii) Order with respect to H$_2$.** Compare experiments 2 and 3: $[\mathrm{NO}]$ is constant (0.3) and $[\mathrm{H_2}]$ is multiplied by 2 ($0.1 \rightarrow 0.2$). The rate is multiplied by 2 ($9 \rightarrow 18$), and $2^1 = 2$. So the reaction is **first order with respect to $\mathrm{H_2}$**.

**(iii) Rate expression.**

$$\text{rate} = k\,[\mathrm{NO}]^2\,[\mathrm{H_2}]$$

(overall order 3; the orders are not the stoichiometric coefficients, which are 2 and 2).

**(iv) Rate constant.** Rearrange: $k = \dfrac{\text{rate}}{[\mathrm{NO}]^2[\mathrm{H_2}]}$.

Experiment 1: $k = \dfrac{1}{(0.1)^2 \times 0.1} = \dfrac{1}{1.0\times10^{-3}} = 1.0\times10^{3}$.

Check with experiment 2: $\dfrac{9}{(0.3)^2 \times 0.1} = \dfrac{9}{9.0\times10^{-3}} = 1.0\times10^{3}$; with experiment 3: $\dfrac{18}{(0.3)^2 \times 0.2} = \dfrac{18}{1.8\times10^{-2}} = 1.0\times10^{3}$. All three agree.

$$k = 1.0\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{dm^6\,mol^{-2}}\ (\text{in units of the relative rate})$$

Because the rate is given only as a relative number, the value of $k$ is relative too. With a rate in $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}\,s^{-1}}$ the units of a third-order constant would be $\mathrm{dm^6\,mol^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A solution, A contains 0.10 mol dm$^{-3}$ of $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$ (ethanoic acid) and 0.20 mol dm$^{-3}$ of $\mathrm{CH_3COONa}$ (Sodium ethanoate).

(i) Give the general name for a solution such as A.

(ii) Give one use of the solution A

(iii) Calculate the pH value of solution A ($K_a$ for $\mathrm{CH_3COOH} = 1.8\times10^{-5}$ mol dm$^{-3}$) *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Solution A, a weak acid with its salt of a strong base, is an **(acidic) buffer solution**: it resists a change of pH when small amounts of acid or alkali are added.

**(ii)** One use (any one): keeping the pH of a medium nearly constant, for example in biochemical and enzyme experiments, in blood and other body fluids (carbonic acid / hydrogencarbonate buffer), in food preservation, or to calibrate a pH meter (standard solution of known pH).

**(iii)** For the weak acid, $\mathrm{CH_3COOH} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3COO^-} + \mathrm{H^+}$:

$$K_a = \frac{[\mathrm{H^+}][\mathrm{CH_3COO^-}]}{[\mathrm{CH_3COOH}]} \quad\Rightarrow\quad [\mathrm{H^+}] = K_a \times \frac{[\mathrm{CH_3COOH}]}{[\mathrm{CH_3COO^-}]}$$

The salt is fully ionised, so $[\mathrm{CH_3COO^-}] \approx [\mathrm{CH_3COONa}] = 0.20\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$; the acid is only slightly ionised (and its ionisation is further suppressed by the common ion), so $[\mathrm{CH_3COOH}] \approx 0.10\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$.

$$[\mathrm{H^+}] = 1.8\times10^{-5} \times \frac{0.10}{0.20} = 9.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$$

$$\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10}(9.0\times10^{-6}) = 5.05$$

Check with the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: $\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a + \log\dfrac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]} = 4.74 + \log 2 = 4.74 + 0.30 = 5.05$.
